title: Inflation among worst and jobless figure rising: IMF
full_text:
Australia is on track for one of the developed world's highest inflation rates next year while also being one of just a handful of countries with rising unemployment, according to International Monetary Fund projections that will intensify pressure on the federal government.
The IMF's latest World Economic Outlook forecasts the nation's inflation will ease from 3.9 per cent this year to 3.1 per cent next year but remain above the Reserve Bank of Australia's target band of 2 per cent to 3 per cent.
That would be the fifth-highest rate among advanced economies, behind Iceland, Greece, Austria and Andorra.
"A prolonged stalemate or further escalation in the Middle East could keep energy and food prices elevated and volatile, revive inflationary pressures, worsen fiscal and external balances and weigh on growth," the IMF wrote, as it urged central banks to maintain a bias towards raising interest rates if they had a long-standing inflation challenge.
Australia's unemployment rate is forecast to rise from 4.4 per cent on average this year to 4.7 per cent next year, the largest increase in percentage-point terms among advanced economies. It is one of just seven advanced economies in which joblessness is projected to rise, although the rate itself is around the average for the group.
Responding to the IMF's projections, Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the global economy was under significant pressure because of the war in the Middle East. "The war is pushing up global inflation while pressures in financial markets, high global debt and reassessments of AI expectations all pose considerable downside risks. We are not immune from these global factors, but we are better placed than many others," Chalmers said.
Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson said the IMF had "called time on the Albanese government's economic model, and the treasurer's spending addiction", which he argued was fuelling inflation and higher interest rates. "This international report card has extraordinarily given the Albanese government two economic 'Fs' and warned if it doesn't kick its spending addiction, Australians will be expelled from prosperity and risk job losses."
Australia has emerged as an economic outlier over the past year. The RBA raised the cash rate to a 15-year high of 4.6 per cent this month as part of its efforts to tame inflation pressures that have dogged the economy since the end of the pandemic.
The minutes of the RBA monetary policy board's September 28 to 29 meeting, released on Tuesday, showed the central bank was prepared to raise the cash rate even further if required to tame price rises.
The latest rate rise means Australia now has the second-highest central bank policy rate in the developed world, behind Iceland.
It has also worsened consumer confidence, which is at its lowest since the early 1990s recession, creating more headwinds for the government as cost-of-living issues loom over parliament.
RBA governor Michele Bullock last month said the jobless rate, which hit 4.6 per cent in August, might need to increase as high as 5 per cent to get inflation under control, sparking outrage among unions, which have been fierce critics of the post-pandemic interest rate rises.
The IMF said higher fuel prices presented a "stagflationary challenge" for energy importers by simultaneously raising headline inflation and depressing output. Although Australia is a major exporter of natural gas and coal, it is reliant on imports of refined fuels including petrol and diesel, for which prices have soared as a result of the conflict in the Middle East.
"Monetary policy can look through the direct effects and possibly short-term indirect effects, but only if the shock is temporary ... and second-round effects, including any sign of de-anchoring inflation expectations, remain contained," said the IMF.
"These conditions are less likely to be satisfied when inflation is already above target and broader price pressures are expected to remain elevated, justifying a bias toward tightening."
The IMF projected that Australian GDP growth would slow to 1.6 per cent in 2027 from 1.9 per cent in 2026 as high interest rates forced a slowdown in household spending.
It said fiscal vulnerabilities and renewed trade tensions could further weaken growth globally, but governments needed not to lose sight of medium-term budget stability.
"Governments should implement credible fiscal adjustment plans that combine enhancements on the revenue side with spending rationalisation, supported by institutional improvements," said the IMF.
"Any support to ease the impact of higher energy and food prices should be temporary, targeted and non-distortionary, and should not jeopardise fiscal sustainability goals."
